stories.headline: The Point Is Open Again
stories.hook: Closed since March for nesting and migrating shorebirds, both beaches at the tip of Cape Henlopen are open again. Here is why it closes, and what the reopening means.
stories.lede: For half the year and more, the very tip of Cape Henlopen belongs to birds. Since Oct. 1, all of it belongs to people again.
stories.body:
For half the year and more, the very tip of Cape Henlopen belongs to birds. Since Oct. 1, all of it belongs to people again.

The Point, the sandy hook at the northern end of Cape Henlopen State Park where the Atlantic meets the mouth of Delaware Bay, closes every year on March 1. It reopens in two stages. This year DNREC reopened the oceanside beach on Tuesday, Sept. 1, to anglers and beachgoers, and kept the bayside beach closed until Thursday, Oct. 1, for shorebirds migrating south.

Why it closes

The Point has closed every March since 1993. The reason is the birds that use it: threatened and endangered beach-nesting and migratory shorebirds, including piping plovers, oystercatchers, least terns and red knots, among other species. In spring and summer the open sand is nesting ground. In late summer and early fall it is a stopping place for birds on their way south, which is why the bayside half stays closed a month longer than the ocean side.

That is the whole logic of the calendar. The closure is not a reaction to any one year's problem. It is the standing arrangement, and it has been for more than three decades.

What reopening means

From now until the end of February, The Point is open on both sides. For anglers it means the oceanside water that was off-limits through the summer is back in play, and the bayside with it since Oct. 1. For everyone else it means the walk out to the tip, where the ocean beach turns the corner into the bay, is possible again.

The fall reopening also lines up with the rest of the season at the park. The fall hawk watch runs at Cape Henlopen through Nov. 30, and after Labor Day the state's drive-on surf fishing rules move into their off-peak season. Both are separate stories, and both are reasons people are at this end of the park in October.

What to keep in mind

The Point is a managed natural area inside a state park, and the closure dates are set by DNREC each year. The dates in this story are this year's. If you are planning a trip around a specific stretch of beach, check the park's current notices before you go; posted closures and fencing on the ground take precedence over anything printed here.

And when March comes around, the tip of the cape closes again, for the same reason it has every year since 1993.

Sources: DNREC news releases of Aug. 25, 2026 (the oceanside reopening on Sept. 1 and the bayside reopening on Oct. 1 for migrating shorebirds) and Feb. 26, 2026 (the March 1 closure). The annual closure since 1993 and the species it protects are as described by DNREC. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit The Point for this story. Park fees, hours and any new closures are set by Delaware State Parks; check the park's current information before you go.

stories.headline: The Off-Season Opens Up the Surf
stories.hook: From the Tuesday after Labor Day until Memorial Day weekend, Delaware's drive-on surf fishing rules ease. Here is what changes, and what never does.
stories.lede: Summer is the hard season for driving onto Delaware's state park beaches to fish. The off-season, which started the Tuesday after Labor Day, is the easy one.
stories.body:
Summer is the hard season for driving onto Delaware's state park beaches to fish. The off-season, which started the Tuesday after Labor Day, is the easy one. Most of what changed is about when you can drive on. Almost nothing changed about what you need to carry, or how you drive once you are there.

What the permit is

A surf fishing vehicle permit lets a vehicle onto designated beaches at Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore and Fenwick Island state parks and at Beach Plum Island Nature Preserve, for one purpose: surf fishing. Permits are issued for the calendar year. They are valid only for two-axle vehicles licensed and registered to drive on public highways.

The purpose rule is strict. Vehicles on the designated beaches are for people actively surf fishing, and driving a permitted vehicle on the beach for anything other than getting to and from fishing is prohibited. The permit is not a pass to park on the sand.

What eased after Labor Day

Reservations. This summer, Delaware State Parks required advance reservations on weekends and holidays at the most popular drive-on beaches: Gordons Pond and Herring Point, Navy Crossing and Point Crossing at Cape Henlopen, and 3Rs at Delaware Seashore. That requirement ran from Saturday, May 23, through Labor Day, Sept. 7, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. The summer reservation window is over.

Off-peak permits. The off-peak surf fishing permit is the one that changes most. In the peak season it allows driving on to fish on weekdays only. In the off-peak season, the Tuesday after Labor Day to Memorial Day weekend, it is valid seven days a week, with no exclusions.

The Point. At the tip of Cape Henlopen, the oceanside beach reopened to anglers and beachgoers on Sept. 1 and the bayside on Oct. 1, after the annual closure for nesting and migrating shorebirds.

What does not change

The equipment rule is year-round. A surf fishing vehicle on state park beaches must carry a shovel, a jack, a tow rope or chain, a board or similar support for the jack, and a low-pressure tire gauge.

So is the driving rule. Vehicles must be driven with regard to existing and potential hazards, and never faster than 15 miles per hour.

And the swimming beaches stay off-limits to vehicles during summer day-use hours. That matters less in October than in July, but it is the same rule when the season turns again.

What this story does not cover

Two things on purpose. Permit prices are set in Delaware State Parks' published rates and fees, and are not repeated here. Fishing regulations themselves, including size and creel limits, are DNREC Division of Fish and Wildlife rules that change by species and season; check them before you keep a fish.

Sources: Delaware State Parks' surf fishing page (permits, designated beaches, vehicle and equipment requirements, the 15 mph limit, the off-peak season); DNREC's May 13, 2026 release on required reservations at the five most popular drive-on beaches (May 23 – Sept. 7, weekends and holidays, 8 a.m.–4 p.m.); DNREC's Aug. 25, 2026 release on The Point's reopening. Delaware Beach Finds did not drive the beaches for this story. Rules and closures can change; Delaware State Parks' current information is the authority.

stories.headline: Apple-Scrapple, Hour by Hour
stories.hook: Bridgeville's 34th Apple-Scrapple Festival starts with a Thursday carnival night and runs through Saturday. Here is the schedule, and the street closures the town has posted.
stories.lede: Bridgeville's Apple-Scrapple Festival is a Friday-and-Saturday street festival with a Thursday-night warm-up, and this year is the 34th.
stories.body:
Bridgeville's Apple-Scrapple Festival is a Friday-and-Saturday street festival with a Thursday-night warm-up, and this year is the 34th. It is organized by the Apple Scrapple Committee, and the official dates are Friday, Oct. 9, and Saturday, Oct. 10.

The name is the program: apples, scrapple, and contests to match.

Thursday, Oct. 8: the warm-up

4 to 9 p.m.: Hometown Carnival Night on Railroad Avenue. This is on the festival's schedule ahead of the two main days.

Friday, Oct. 9: opening night

  • 4 p.m.: The bandstand, carnival and food court open.
  • 4 to 6 p.m.: RAPA sampling event at RAPA.
  • 5 to 6 p.m.: Kids Apple Toss registration at the bandstand.
  • 6 p.m.: Opening ceremony at the bandstand.
  • 6:15 p.m.: Little Miss Apple Scrapple Pageant.
  • 7 p.m.: Kids Apple Toss.
  • 8:30 to 10 p.m.: Friday Night Street Dance.
  • 10 p.m.: Bandstand, carnival and food court close.

Saturday, Oct. 10: the main day

The festival opens at 9 a.m., with music at the bandstand through the day. Two of Saturday's contests:

  • 1 p.m.: Ladies Skillet Toss, in the Union Methodist Church lot. Registration runs 12:40 to 12:55.
  • 2 to 3 p.m.: Invitational Scrapple Sling, at the bandstand.

The festival's own schedule page has the full bandstand lineup and the rest of the day's events; it is the one to check on the morning you go.

The street closures

The Town of Bridgeville has posted its festival traffic plan, and this year it includes more street closures. The parts most likely to matter to visitors:

  • Market Street is closed to all traffic except buses from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10.
  • Delaware Avenue, the 300 and 400 blocks, is closed to all traffic from 6 a.m. to midnight on Saturday.
  • No parking is permitted in front of residences on Delaware Avenue, Walnut Street, South Cannon Street (Market to Cedar), Laws Street (Market to Edgewood) and Williams Street from 8 a.m. Friday, Oct. 9, until 8 a.m. Sunday, Oct. 11. Mill, John, Mechanic and Cedar streets and Cherry Lane are also on the closure list.

Residents have to have vehicles off the street by 6 a.m. Saturday or they will be towed at the owner's expense. Visitor parking arrangements are not part of the town's notice, so plan your arrival with the festival's directions page rather than expecting to park on the closed streets.

Sources: The Bridgeville Apple-Scrapple Festival's 2026 schedule (applescrapple.com) for the Thursday, Friday and Saturday times and locations; the Town of Bridgeville's 2026 Apple Scrapple Festival resident updates (bridgeville.delaware.gov) for the 34th edition, the Oct. 9–10 dates and the street closures and parking restrictions. Delaware Beach Finds did not attend. Schedules can change; check the festival's own pages before you go.

stories.headline: The Last Lightship
stories.hook: The lightship in Lewes was built in Maine in 1938 and spent its working life off New England. How it came to carry a Delaware Bay name is the story of a station, a historical society and a one-dollar sale.
stories.lede: The ship called Overfalls never stood the Overfalls station. It carries the name in honor of it.
stories.body:
The ship called Overfalls never stood the Overfalls station. It carries the name in honor of it, and the story of how that happened runs from a Maine shipyard to a one-dollar sale in Lewes.

What a lightship was

A lightship did a lighthouse's job from a fixed point on the water, where building a tower was not possible. It was a ship that stayed put. The one now in Lewes, designated LV-118, was the last lightship built for the U.S. Lighthouse Service.

Built in Maine, 1938

LV-118 was built in 1938 at the Rice Brothers shipyard in East Boothbay, Maine. It incorporated what was then the latest in lightship design, including steel bulkheads that divided the hull into compartments.

Thirty-four years off New England

Its working life was spent at three stations far from Delaware:

  • 1938 to 1957: Cornfield Point, Connecticut.
  • 1958 to 1962: Cross Rip, near Cape Cod, Massachusetts.
  • 1962 to 1972: Boston.

In 1972 it was taken out of service. Along the way it also carried the Coast Guard designation WAL-539.

A Delaware name

In 1973 the Coast Guard donated the ship to the Lewes Historical Society to serve as a floating museum. It was given a new name, Overfalls, in honor of the lightship station closest to Lewes, at the mouth of Delaware Bay. The ship in Lewes is, in that sense, a memorial to a station as much as a vessel with its own history.

The one-dollar sale

Keeping a historic steel ship afloat is a long job. A group called the Friends of the Lightship formed inside the historical society and later incorporated as an independent nonprofit foundation, which bought the ship for one dollar. Its mission, in the foundation's telling, was plain: save the ship, make it sustainable and put it in a proper setting. On Dec. 7, 2001, ownership passed to the Overfalls Maritime Museum Foundation.

The ship has since been designated a National Historic Landmark.

Seeing it

The Overfalls is one of the landmarks tied to Lewes's Maritime Weekend, when the Boast the Coast festival offered free visits and tours associated with the ship on Oct. 3. Its regular open days and hours are set by the foundation and change with the season; check the Overfalls Foundation's own schedule before you plan a visit.

Sources: The Overfalls Foundation's history of the ship (overfalls.org) for its construction, design, stations, the 1973 donation and renaming, the Friends of the Lightship and the 2001 transfer; the Delaware Public Archives historical marker for Lightship Overfalls (archives.delaware.gov); the Historical Marker Database transcription. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit the ship for this story. Visiting days and hours are the foundation's; check its current schedule.

stories.headline: Delaware's State Parks Turn 75
stories.hook: In 1951, Delaware authorized three state parks. Seventy-five years later the system protects more than 27,000 acres, including the long state park beaches at Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore and Fenwick Island.
stories.lede: Delaware's state park system is 75 years old this year, and it began with three parks.
stories.body:
Delaware's state park system is 75 years old this year, and it began with three parks.

1951

The system dates to 1951, when Delaware's legislature authorized three state parks: Trap Pond, Fort Delaware and Brandywine Springs.

2026

What began with three parks is now a system of 17 state parks and 22 nature preserves, along with the Brandywine Zoo and the Indian River Marina. Together they protect more than 27,000 acres.

For anyone who knows Delaware from its coast, several of its best-known places are state parks. Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore and Fenwick Island state parks, and Beach Plum Island Nature Preserve, are where the state's designated surf fishing beaches are. Cape Henlopen is home to the fall hawk watch and to The Point, which reopened for the season on Oct. 1.

How the anniversary is being marked

Delaware State Parks has spread the 75th anniversary across the whole year rather than a single day:

  • First Day Hikes on New Year's Day kicked the anniversary year off.
  • A Day of Service on the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. holiday, Jan. 19, was the first of four signature service days. The others are tied to Earth Day in April, the anniversary month of June, and a Fall Service Day.
  • The fee season that began March 1 was billed as the start of a year of anniversary events and activities.
  • The Parks for Everyone 5K, a virtual fundraiser, invites people to run, walk or roll the trails to raise money for future programs.
  • A goal to plant 75,000 trees, reforesting land and cleared meadows, as part of the parks' strategic plan and DNREC's Tree for Every Delawarean Initiative.

The part still to come

The Fall Service Day is the anniversary event most likely to be ahead of you this season. Delaware State Parks publishes its date and locations on its 75th anniversary page; that, rather than any date printed here, is the one to check.

Seventy-five years on, the system that started with three parks reaches the ocean at Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore and Fenwick Island.

Sources: Delaware State Parks' "Our Story" and 75th anniversary pages (destateparks.com) for the 1951 founding, the three original parks and today's system; DNREC releases of Dec. 30, 2025 (First Day Hikes), Jan. 14, 2026 (Day of Service and the four service days), Feb. 24, 2026 (fee season and anniversary events) and June 22, 2026 (the Parks for Everyone 5K); Delaware State Parks' Tree Titans page for the 75,000-tree goal. Delaware Beach Finds did not attend anniversary events for this story.

stories.headline: The Jazz Festival Comes Back to Rehoboth
stories.hook: The 37th Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival runs Thursday through Sunday, Oct. 15–18, on stages across Rehoboth, Lewes and Dewey. Who is playing, and where to find the schedule.
stories.lede: The Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival is in its 37th year, and it runs Thursday through Sunday this week.
stories.body:
The Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival is in its 37th year, and it runs Thursday through Sunday this week: Oct. 15 to 18.

The festival dates to 1990, and this year's edition spreads across five stages in Rehoboth Beach, Lewes and Dewey Beach, including the Rehoboth Beach Convention Center.

Who is playing

The festival books nationally known jazz, smooth jazz and R&B artists. This year's announced headliners include:

  • Brian Culbertson
  • Boney James
  • Damien Escobar
  • Najee
  • Gerald Albright
  • Walter Beasley

Stanley Jordan and Paul Taylor are among the many other artists on the bill.

How to plan it

Four days and five stages means the festival is better approached as a set of individual shows than as a single event. The festival's own schedule and tickets page lists every performance by day, venue and time; it is the only place to plan from, and the one place for prices, which this story deliberately does not quote.

The City of Rehoboth Beach lists the festival on its own events calendar for the same Oct. 15–18 dates.

The rest of October

The jazz festival is the middle of a busy month at the coast. A week later, Rehoboth's Sea Witch weekend brings a first-year Community Fair for local nonprofits on Friday, Oct. 23, and the costume parade on Saturday, Oct. 24. Times for Sea Witch had not been confirmed when this was published; check the Rehoboth Beach-Dewey Beach Chamber of Commerce before you plan around them.

Sources: The Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival's schedule and tickets pages (rehobothjazz.com); the City of Rehoboth Beach's events calendar listing (rehobothbeachde.gov); the Cape Gazette's report "Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival to return Oct. 15–18" and WMDT's Discover Delmarva Arts feature, which both report the 2026 headliners; the Rehoboth Beach-Dewey Beach Chamber's Sea Witch listing for the Oct. 23 and 24 dates. Delaware Beach Finds did not attend. Line-ups and times can change; the festival's own schedule is the authority.

stories.headline: The Warship That Went Down Off Cape Henlopen
stories.hook: On May 25, 1798, the British warship DeBraak capsized in a sudden squall off Cape Henlopen. Almost two centuries later its hull came back up, and Delaware has looked after it ever since.
stories.lede: On the afternoon of May 25, 1798, the British warship DeBraak capsized and sank off Cape Henlopen.
stories.body:
On the afternoon of May 25, 1798, the British warship DeBraak capsized and sank off Cape Henlopen. She had been escorting and protecting a convoy of British and American merchant ships bound for the United States when a sudden squall caught her.

The loss

DeBraak was commanded by James Drew of the Royal Navy, and he was among those lost. How many died with him is one of the details on which accounts disagree. A state historical marker gives thirty-three of an eighty-five-man crew. Other accounts put it at thirty-five crew plus a dozen Spanish prisoners on board, or at forty-seven lost in all. The local pilot, Andrew Allen, survived, according to the historical marker.

The disagreement is worth saying out loud rather than smoothing over. A wreck two and a quarter centuries old reaches us through records that do not always agree, and this one is no exception.

Raised in 1986

For nearly two hundred years the wreck stayed on the bottom off Lewes. In August 1986 a private salvage company raised the hull from the ocean floor. The raising was a commercial operation, and it badly damaged what was left of the ship.

Altogether more than 20,000 artifacts were recovered from the wreck site, along with roughly a third of the ship's lower hull.

Delaware's collection

The state held passive custody of the collection from 1986 and in 1992 bought it outright from the salvage company. Since then the remaining section of the hull and the artifact collection have been curated by the Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs. The hull itself is kept at a conservation facility near Cape Henlopen State Park.

The Division's Zwaanendael Museum, at 102 Kings Highway in Lewes, has made the DeBraak a recurring subject of its exhibitions and programs over the years.

Seeing it

The Division runs free "Walk to the DeBraak" tours of the hull, for groups of up to 18 visitors ages 10 and up. Dates are set by the Division; the Zwaanendael Museum is the place to ask about the next one.

Sources: Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs, "Remembering the HMS DeBraak 225 Years Later" (2023) and "Caring for the HMS DeBraak" (2022), for the convoy, the date, the 1986 salvage, the artifact count, the 1992 purchase and the Division's curation; State of Delaware News on the Zwaanendael Museum's DeBraak exhibitions; the Division's "Walk to the DeBraak" tour listing for the tour format; the H.M. Brig DeBraak historical marker and other accounts for the casualty figures, which disagree. Delaware Beach Finds has not toured the hull.
